title: common.v1: definitions shared by the control records
description: Shared definitions. Nothing here is a record on its own; the record schemas beside this file refer to these by '$ref': 'common.v1.json#/$defs/<name>'. Every string pattern is written for ECMA 262 and is paired with a 'not' that refuses a line break, because some regular expression engines let '$' match before a final newline.

run_id.description: Names one run. A run is one supervised unit with its own Stop. The daemon accepts 1 to 64 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 _ and -; the control API mints 'run-' followed by 32 hex digits.

session_id.description: Names one session. Minted by the core. Always starts with 'ses-'.

log_id.description: Names one event log. It is a session id, or, for a run that was started without a session, 'run:' followed by that run's id. Sequence numbers are counted per log.

turn_id.description: Names one turn. A turn is one input and the engine's work until it yields. Minted by the core. Always starts with 'turn-'.

item_id.description: Names one queued message. Minted by the core. Always starts with 'qi-'.

delivery_id.description: Names one attempt to hand a message to an engine. Minted by the core when delivery begins, written toward the engine with the message, and named again by the event that shows the engine took it. Always starts with 'dlv-'.

approval_id.description: Names one approval request. Minted by the core, never by an engine or a plugin. Always starts with 'apr-'.

command_id.description: A client's own id for one mutating request, so a retry is recognised. Minted by the client: at least 96 bits of randomness, or a random part made once per client process followed by a counter. 8 to 128 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : and -.

token.description: A short opaque reference: 1 to 128 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : and -.

sha256.description: A SHA-256 digest as 64 lower-case hex digits.

timestamp.description: A moment in UTC as RFC 3339 with exactly three decimal places and a 'Z', for example 2026-11-13T07:40:00.000Z. Every record that is new in version 1 uses this form. Every field typed timestamp is a real UTC calendar instant under the declared millisecond spelling: a pattern cannot say that February has no 31st, so the keyword 'x-instant' says it, and the conformance client checks it (conformance/wire_client.py). A validator that does not know that keyword ignores it and must make the check itself. The real-instant check validates the seconds spelling as well as the calendar date. A :60 spelling is accepted only for an actual UTC leap second supported by the timestamp profile; it is not normalized from an arbitrary minute into its successor. Otherwise it is refused as timestamp. THE PROFILE OF THESE RECORDS SUPPORTS NO LEAP SECOND: seconds are 00 to 59, in the pattern and in the check, so every :60 is refused, on a day that had a leap second as on any other. The core's clocks do not produce one.

epoch_seconds.description: A moment as Unix seconds with a fraction. Only the stored run record uses this form, because that is what the registry has written since before version 1.

seq.description: A position in one event log. The first event of a log is 1 and each later event is one more: there are no holes, and a number is never used twice.

revision.description: Counts the changes to one record. It starts at 1 and rises by one with every change. A mutating request names the revision it read; a request that names an older one is refused 'conflict'.

epoch.description: The daemon's epoch: a whole number that only rises, by one each time a daemon opens the event store. A cursor carries it so a client can tell that the daemon restarted between two reads.

tenant.description: The tenant a run or session belongs to, as run.start takes it today: any non-empty string.

engine_name.description: An engine's name in the engine table, for example claude_code, codex or recursion_loop. Lower-case letters, digits and underscores, at most 32 characters, starting with a letter.

code_word.description: A typed code: lower-case letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter.

connection.description: The login or key a route is billed through: its kind, and a label for it. The label is never a credential and never contains one.

connection_id.description: A connection written as one string, '<kind>:<id>': the key the breaker and the meters use (routes/contract.py, connection_key). A label, never a credential.

principal.description: Who asked. 'owner' is the user on the owner-only socket; 'device' is a paired device on the page's door; 'session' is an engine acting with a token scoped to its own session; 'plugin' is a loaded plugin; 'internal' is the daemon's own code. The server derives the principal from the way the request came in; it is never read from the request. The id is a label for that principal. A token, a cookie or a key never appears here.

owner.description: Who owns a run: 'host' (the core, for a run a user or a session started) or the id of the plugin that started it. Derived by the server from the principal, never taken from a request.

workspace.description: Where a session or run works. 'path' is the launch folder the user chose. In 'direct' mode the engine works in that folder and worktree_path is null. In 'worktree' mode the engine works in worktree_path, a git worktree cut from base_ref, and both are strings.

route.description: A route in short: the engine, the model (null when the engine's own default is used) and the connection it is billed through. The stored run record keeps more (run.record.v1, launch_route): everything the launch used.

hand_pick.description: The route the user named. A hand pick always wins over the routing config and the default.

route_decision.description: What routing decided, and why. chosen is the route. reason is 'hand_pick' (the user named it), 'config' (the routing config chose it) or 'default' (the default engine). candidates lists every route that was considered, in order; 'skipped' is null for the one chosen and otherwise a typed code for why it was passed over. hand_pick is what the user named, or null.

budget.description: The most a run or a session may spend, in US dollars. 0 means nothing may be spent, and that is the default: a record with no budget is read as cap_usd 0. The reservation itself, with its id and its state, is kept in the quota ledger under the run's id and is not written into any record here. A budget never carries or names a key.

lease.description: Who holds the run for now. owner labels the holder, epoch is the daemon epoch it was taken in, and after expires_at another holder may take it.

cgroup_identity.description: The identity of a unit's cgroup directory as the kernel gives it: the device and inode numbers read at launch. A path can be reused; this pair is how a later check tells the same directory from a new one at the same path.

cursor.description: A client's place in one event log: the epoch it read in, the log, and the last sequence number it has (0 before the first event). The request cursor's session_id identifies the one requested log, and authorization is checked for that log. Every returned event or transcript line belongs to it. Return only positions strictly after cursor.seq, in order. Every skipped retained-log position is represented by the prescribed replay.gap; projection does not silently filter positions. A gap has from <= to, starts at the next missing position, and has envelope seq equal to to. The response cursor is the last represented position, or the unchanged input position for an empty response. Its log ID never changes. A first read uses epoch 1 and seq 0. An older epoch continues on the same persistent log sequence and returns the current epoch with epoch_advanced=true. Equal epoch returns epoch_advanced=false. A future epoch is request_invalid with detail cursor_epoch_ahead. A seq beyond the current high-water mark is request_invalid with detail cursor_ahead; a seq at the high-water mark is a valid empty read or follow wait. An existing empty log accepts seq 0; an unknown log returns session_unknown. Epoch 1 is the minimum/bootstrap token, not a claim that the client previously observed the log. epoch_advanced is true exactly when a successful continuation replaces an older requested epoch with the current one; it is not a reset-to-zero instruction. A cursor is the only thing a read names, so a cursor of another log is a request for that other log: a client stores its cursors per log and checks that the cursor it sends is the one of the log it means to read; the server authorizes the log the cursor names and never splices another log into the answer. A successful events.read or events.follow response uses the projection explicitly requested by the caller. Validate that equality before checking the returned page. When projection is omitted, the method must document one default and test it. A transcript page is produced only from a raw page whose log identity, sequence continuity and gap bounds have already been validated. A transcript line's missing log and gap-start fields do not waive those producer checks. The default is raw. conformance/rules.py (cursor_answer, page_problems, transcript_page_problems) states this as code; the vectors in vectors/event.cursor and vectors/event.page check it.
